_doc.purpose: Where each silhouette class is plausible, and how it groups. The tunable art layer; scripts/ocean-asset-facts.json holds the objective half.
_doc.substrate: Derived by scripts/ocean-terrain-sampler.cjs from terrain shape: sand | reef | rock.
_doc.slopeRange: Degrees off horizontal. Substrate above 35 is always rock, so a class admitting rock needs the range to reach it.
_doc.depthBand: Metres below the water plane (z = +12). Minimum 1 everywhere keeps things underwater: the upstage wall crest breaks the surface.
_doc.habit: solitary places one; clumping scatters siblings around a seed; colonial packs a dense mat.
_doc.companionSpacing: Multiples of footprint radius, enforced against same-class neighbours.
_doc.tiltJitter: Degrees of random tilt off the substrate normal.

roleAdmits._doc: Which silhouette classes each zone role may draw from. Zones own staging and sightlines; this is where the theatre overrides the biology. A reef that composed itself purely from ecology would put a pinnacle in front of the stage.

plate.notes: Tables and fans need hard substrate and near-flat ground; a table coral on a 30-degree face reads as debris.

branching.notes: Staghorn grows in thickets. A single isolated staghorn is the tell that a reef was placed by a random walk.

mound.notes: Massive corals are slow and old. They earn space around them; crowding them reads as fake.

column.notes: Pinnacles are landmarks at 6-12 m. Two adjacent ones cancel each other out as landmarks. Admits reef as well as rock: substrate 'rock' is derived from slope above 35 degrees, so rock alone plus a 30-degree cap can never be satisfied.

blade.notes: Kelp and grass are beds, not specimens. Dense, aligned to the current, on soft ground.

boulder.notes: Rock does not care which way it sits. Heavy tilt jitter is what stops a boulder field looking placed.

shell.notes: Small sand detail. Collects in flat ground, never on a slope it would roll off. Tilt was 20, which contradicted that note and stood 39 starfish and shells up on their edges -- a starfish is a 3.44 x 0.63 disc, so 20 degrees of jitter is the difference between lying on the sand and leaning against it.

outcrop.notes: Jointed volcanic bedrock breaking through the seabed -- the substrate the reef is built on, which across the volcanic tropics is what reefs actually grow on. Columnar jointing cracks PERPENDICULAR to the cooling surface, so on a flat floor the columns stand vertical: tilt is near zero, and a leaning basalt mass is the one thing this rock never does. It also never appears alone -- colonnades, walls, cliff faces -- hence a clump of 3-5. Distinct from 'boulder', whose whole character is 25 degrees of 'rock does not care which way it sits'; that rule applied to basalt is what produced a 12.9 m block lying over at 27 degrees.

arch.notes: An arch only works if you can see through it. Camera-biased yaw is load-bearing, not a nicety.

wall.notes: Buttresses frame. They face the audience or they are a slab seen edge-on.

swimmer.notes: Pelagic: hovers above the floor rather than sitting on it. The generator lifts these off the terrain.

crawler.notes: Bottom-dwelling animals: they SIT on the substrate like scenery does, which is the whole reason they cannot be 'swimmer'. The generator lifts a swimmer 1.2-4.0 m off the floor, so classing a blue-spotted ray and a common octopus as swimmers hovered a ray 3.2 m and an octopus 3.5 m above the sand -- both of which spend their lives against it. Solitary to a pair; an octopus does not school.

wreck.notes: One wreck is a story. Two is a shipping lane.
